questions.q: How do you turn on the actual execution plan in SSMS before running a query?
options: Click Include Actual Execution Plan on the toolbar, or press Ctrl+M
It's on by default for every query
Right-click the Results grid after running the query
Type SET SHOWPLAN ON as the first line of the query
questions.explain: Ctrl+M (or the toolbar button) tells SSMS to capture and display the real execution plan alongside Results and Messages.

questions.q: What does an Index Seek mean?
options: SQL Server used the index's B-tree to jump straight to the needed rows
SQL Server read every row in the table in order
The query failed and had to retry
The index was rebuilt before the query ran
questions.explain: A seek navigates the index tree directly to matching rows — the fast path when an index is usable.

questions.q: Is an Index Scan always a performance problem?
options: No — a query that genuinely needs most of the table can be cheaper to scan than to seek row-by-row
Yes — every scan should be eliminated
No — scans and seeks always cost exactly the same
Yes — a scan means the query returned incorrect results
questions.explain: The red flag is a scan against a large table when only a few rows were actually needed, not a scan by itself.

questions.q: In the lab, what turned the Clustered Index Scan into an Index Seek?
options: Creating a nonclustered index on the Name column used in the WHERE clause
Adding a second WHERE condition
Restarting SQL Server
Switching from SELECT * to naming columns
questions.explain: Once an index existed on Name, SQL Server could navigate directly to the matching rows instead of scanning every row.

questions.q: What does an operator's Cost % represent in an execution plan?
options: Its share of the total estimated cost of the whole query
The exact number of milliseconds it took to run
The percentage of CPU cores used
How much disk space the operator's data occupies
questions.explain: Cost % is relative to the query's total estimated cost — it points you toward which operator deserves tuning attention first.
